submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on the function word that opens a definite reference to members of an organised collective - most strongly the article in partitive phrases ('one / two / several / many / some of the X'), also 'all' + plural noun and '<verb> as <designation>' - and its strength roughly doubles when a collective entity (club, firm, team, church) has been named in the preceding ~15 tokens rather than a mere object (ship, rock, tree). It never peaks on the head noun (which it cannot see), stays near zero on demonstratives ('one of those X'), on genitive 'of' ('a member of the X') and on bare definites ('the members'), and ablating it lowers the probability of collective nouns (club, team, church, NFL); the protocol's lookahead gate still returns retrospective (KL 6.3e-4, just under its 1e-3 threshold).

The Huffington Post: Top Design Destinations for 2017

2017-02-23

By Janette Ewen

Ever since Frank Gehry’s spectacular Guggenheim Bilbao put its sleepy namesake city on the radar of architecture buffs two decades ago, design has became an integral aspect of travel and tourism, joining food, culture and climate when it comes to visitor draws. This year, the list of destinations sure to entice design fans includes spots from the West Indies to North Africa. They offer a wide range of aesthetic attractions, from cutting-edge urban design to exquisite historical gems.

OLD HAVANA, NEW URGENCY

Whether the recent detente between the United States and Cuba will result in an onslaught of American visitors to the island or not, Canadians aren’t waiting to find out: According to KAYAK, a world-leading travel search engine, Havana is one of the year’s top 10 trending destinations among travellers from the Great White North, whose online inquiries about the city skyrocketed by 230 percent compared to last year. In anticipation of more visitors, hotels in Havana are being modernized and restaurants given new polish, but it’s the bustling metropolis’ status as a living design museum that no doubt appeals to most foreigners. For architecture fans, hotels like the Nacional offer glimpses into long-gone eras, while automobile buffs would be hard-pressed to find a greater parade of vintage cars. Speaking of moveable feasts, bars like La Floridita, where Ernest Hemingway indulged his fondness for daiquiris, are modern-day links to literary and artistic legends. Clearly, the time to visit Havana is now, whatever your aesthetic bent.

CARIBBEAN COOL

Over the past several years, restaurant-rich Grand Cayman, the largest of the Cayman Islands, has been nurturing a reputation as the culinary capital of the Caribbean. Now, its growing foodie cred is being matched by its design cachet. In November, the ultra-sleek Kimpton Seafire Resort + Spa, designed by U.S. firm SB Architects, opened on Seven Mile Beach, bringing a welcome shot of global chic (plus four more dining options) to that pristine stretch of coastline. Not far away, Camana Bay, an ambitious mixed-use development, has been heralded as a rare example of new urbanism in the region, its 500 acres encompassing high-end shops, office and residential space, interactive fountains and a pedestrianized main street called the Paseo. Situated between the Kimpton and Camana Bay is the Caribbean Club, a luxury apartment hotel and ideal base for exploring the area; it also houses one of Grand Cayman’s foremost eateries, the trattoria Luca.

Connect The Dots

In her firstbook Stay Hungry Stay Foolish Rashmi Bansal profiled twenty five entrepreneurs who were alumni of IIM – Ahmedabad. Many had then wondered including yours truly, how important an MBA degree is to become an entrepreneur. Rashmi claims this inspired her to write Connect The Dots, story of twenty one entrepreneurs but who dont have an MBA degree. The format of the book is same as her last book. There are twenty chapters, one on each entrepreneur (Gaurav Rathore & Saurabh Vyas who co founded PoliticalEDGE are covered in one chapter) and the entire chapter is based on one single interview.

The book is divided in three sections : Jugaad, Junoon & Zubaan. Jugaadis are those who didn’t get any formal training in business but learned by observing, experimenting and applying their mind. It includes some one like Kunwer Sachdev of Su-Kam who created a Rs 500 crore company from scratch; Ganesh Ram, who started what is today India’s largest English training academy, VETA when there were no BPOs and no one knew that English coaching would be as big a market as it is now.

Junoonis as the name suggests, are passionate about something that is ahead of its time. This was my favorite section in the book. Gaurav Rathore and Saurabh Vyas envisioned a consulting and research firm exclusively for politics and founded PoliticalEDGE; Satyajit Singh, founder of Shakti Sudha not only created a new industry but also benefited thousands of farmers in rural Bihar; Chetan Maini, founder of Reva, designed a solar car and has been producing electric cars since the time when global warming was not so well known and creating electric cars seemed to make little sense.

The third section Zubaan is about creative people like Paresh Mokashi, creator of Harishchandrachi Factory, India’s official entry to Oscar last year or Krishna Reddy, whose Prince Dance Group, consisting of daily wage laborers won India’s Got Talent last year.

I had great hopes from the book as I loved Stay Hungry Stay Foolish. The first chapter on Prem Ganpathy is literally a rags to riches story of someone who came to Mumbai with no money and now owns Dosa Plaza, a fast food chain with 26 outlets in the country.The rest of the stories too are very encouraging. The book is replete with inspiring anecdotes and quotes . When I read the synopsis on the third section i.e. Zubaan, I thought it would be probably the weak link in this book as stories on creatives who had made it big in the field of art would be a misfit in this book about entrepreneurs. However, all these artists achieved commercial success by following their passion and this justifies their inclusion in this book about Entrepreneurs. Entrepreneurship after all is about following your heart.

Germany and China are finding out the hard way that switching to renewables isn’t as simple as building more wind turbines and solar panels.

The Guardian reports that leaked plans from the German federal network agency, which manages the country’s power grid, describe how it is planning to cut back its ambitions for wind power in the north of the country because the grid can’t handle it. Wind turbines have been going up rapidly in the north, with the intention of supplying energy to engineering hubs in the south. But recently the government has had to pay wind power providers to reduce their generation because its energy grid is at full capacity. The leaked papers suggest that Germany will halve its wind turbine expansion plans as a result.

A similar story is playing out in China. According to a BBC report, the country has built so many coal-fired power plants, which are slow to turn on and off, that it has to turn its wind turbines off for as much as 15 percent of the time because its grid can’t always handle both being online concurrently. It’s not the first time that China’s renewables eyes have proven bigger than its grid belly, either: it’s been adding solar power installations so fast that it can’t make use of as much as 50 percent of the energy being generated in some provinces.

This is a problem that’s likely to rear its head again and again. India and Australia are both under increasing pressure to build out their grid infrastructure to support renewables. The most impressive example of wind power adoption in the U.S. has played out in, of all places, Texas. It’s only been made possible by a gigantic transmission system that was built to take electricity from the desolate northwest portion of the state to the big cities in the southeast. But it cost $7 billion—a price that could be prohibitive in other regions.

In this, there is a lesson. Swift adoption of renewables is laudable—but only if it’s done in such a way that the resulting energy can be used.

(Read more: BBC, The Guardian, “China’s Solar Binge Is Turning Into a Hangover,” “The One and Only Texas Wind Boom,” “Renewables Are Booming—but Buyer Beware”)

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Several of those clubs in the league have already announced new head coaches for next season, and the supporters are still arguing about the choices on every forum.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The hypothesis explicitly predicts near zero on demonstrative partitives such as 'one of those X', so this 'several of those clubs' near-miss should not fire despite matching the determiner, the partitive structure and the collective noun.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She has been a loyal member of the Riverside Rowing Club for more than twenty years and still coaches the novice crews on weekend mornings.
adversarial_test_results.detail: This is the genitive 'of' ('a member of the X') that the hypothesis says stays near zero, even though it names an organised club and contains both 'of' and 'the'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The members of the committee gathered in the hall at seven o'clock to review the annual budget and the proposed fee increase for next year.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The hypothesis predicts near zero on bare definites ('the members'), even when the head noun is the plural of a collective's members.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The committee will publish its findings next month, according to a statement released by the chair on Tuesday.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A collective noun under a definite article with no reference to its members should be near zero, since the hypothesis says the pole fires on member-referring function words and never peaks on the head noun.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The old fishing boat was moored at the end of the pier, its paint peeling after decades of salt air and winter storms.
adversarial_test_results.detail: An ordinary definite article before a singular, non-collective object is the baseline the hypothesis says should stay near zero.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He was all set to leave when the mechanic called to say the car in the garage would not be ready until Friday afternoon.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed token 'all' here is a degree adverb, not 'all' + plural noun, so the hypothesis predicts no activation despite the surface match.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The river runs as straight as an arrow through the valley before it bends toward the sea near the old mill.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed token 'as' appears twice in an 'as ... as' comparative rather than a '<verb> as <designation>' frame, which the hypothesis says should not fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: As the team bus pulled out of the stadium, the coach waved to the few supporters who had waited by the gate in the rain.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Here 'as' is a temporal subordinator and a collective ('team', 'coach') is nearby, so this is the strongest wrong-sense test of the '<verb> as <designation>' claim.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: /* Returns the number of open sockets; call this with care after the listener has been shut down. */
adversarial_test_results.detail: A code comment matching the genre of the top examples but containing only 'the' and 'with' before non-collective nouns, which the hypothesis predicts stays near zero.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: All of the furniture in the lounge was replaced last spring, but the faded carpet and the old clock stayed where they were.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The hypothesis restricts 'all' activation to 'all' + plural noun, so this mass-noun 'all of the' near-miss should not fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: We need more time to finish the report, and a few more people on the review panel would help us meet the deadline.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed token 'more' is a comparative quantifier with no partitive 'of the', so the hypothesis predicts near zero.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The primary reason for the delay was a faulty sensor in the cooling system, according to the maintenance log.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed token 'primary' is an ordinary adjective with no definite member reference, which the hypothesis does not predict to fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She ordered a regular coffee and sat by the window of the diner, watching the traffic on the street outside.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed token 'regular' is a noun-modifying adjective here rather than the nominal 'regulars' of example 1, so the hypothesis predicts no activation.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The board of the local football club met on Thursday evening. Several of the directors wanted to delay the vote on the new stadium until the spring.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A partitive 'several of the' whose article opens a reference to the club's members, with the collective 'club' named eight tokens earlier, is exactly the boosted pattern the hypothesis predicts should fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
By the middle of the nineteenth century the harbour at Port Ellen had become the busiest on the western coast. Every morning before dawn the fishing fleet left the shelter of the breakwater, and every evening the crews returned to gut and salt their catch on the stone quay. The town had grown around that trade. Coopers, rope-makers, sail-makers and merchants kept shops within sight of the water, and their sons were expected to follow them into the same work. It was a closed world, and everyone in it knew everyone else's business.

The Merchants' Guild had been founded in 1807, when a group of wealthy traders petitioned the town council for the right to set prices at the weekly market. For the first forty years the guild concerned itself with little more than weights and measures and the licensing of stalls. Its meetings were short, its records dull, and its influence hardly reached beyond the market square. The real power in Port Ellen lay with the shipowners, whose vessels carried coal south and brought grain and timber north, and with the harbourmaster, who decided which ships docked first and which waited at anchor for days.

That balance began to shift in the 1850s, when the railway reached the town and the old coastal trade started to shrink. The shipowners, facing cheaper competition from the larger ports, cut wages and laid off hands. The guild, which had never taken much interest in labour questions, suddenly found itself the only institution in Port Ellen with the standing to speak for the men who unloaded the cargo. Its membership swelled. Clerks, carters, coopers and even some smaller shopkeepers began attending its meetings, and the old guard of merchants found themselves outvoted on questions they had once settled privately over dinner.

The council elections of 1872 gave the guild its first seat in the town hall, and the men who had spent their lives hauling timber suddenly found themselves drafting regulations about drainage and street lighting. The old merchants complained that the guild had forgotten its purpose. The new members replied that the purpose had always been to protect the trade of the town, and that the trade could not be protected by men who had never lifted a crate. The argument was never settled; it simply moved from the meeting room into the pages of the local paper, where it continued for the rest of the decade.

The crisis came in the spring of 1874. The shipowners announced a cut in the loading rates, and the guild called an emergency meeting in the corn exchange. Some of the members wanted an immediate strike, while others urged negotiation and pointed to the savings the men had put aside during the good years. The debate ran past midnight. In the end the guild voted narrowly to send a delegation to the harbourmaster and to ask the town council to arbitrate. The shipowners refused to meet the delegation for three weeks, and by the time they agreed the loading season was half over.

The settlement, when it came, satisfied nobody. The rates were restored, but the guild had to promise that its members would not stop work again during the harvest. The merchants who had founded the guild forty years earlier were appalled at what their institution had become. Several resigned their seats and withdrew their subscriptions. The younger members, who now made up the majority, cared little for their disapproval. They had discovered that an organisation built to regulate market stalls could, with a little patience, be turned into something much more useful.

By 1880 the guild had its own newspaper, a reading room above the corn exchange, and a fund for the widows of men lost at sea. It had also acquired a reputation in the county for stubbornness. When the railway company tried to raise its freight charges, the guild organised a boycott that lasted a whole winter, and the company eventually backed down. Visitors from London remarked on how well the town's working men were organised, and several wrote articles marvelling at the sight of coopers debating procedure with the same gravity as lawyers.

Nothing lasts forever. The harbour silted up in the 1890s, the railway took the trade inland, and the guild's membership dwindled year by year. Its last recorded meeting was held in the corn exchange in 1911, with eleven men present and no business to discuss. The building itself was pulled down in the 1930s, and a cinema now stands where the merchants once argued about the price of oats. Yet the records survive, bound in green cloth and stored in the county archive, and historians who read them are still struck by how quickly a modest association of shopkeepers learned to act like a government.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A roughly 900-token historical essay, a genre absent from the examples, whose only member-referring 'of the' partitive is 'Some of the members' about 600 tokens in, where the guild has been named repeatedly and the hypothesis predicts the collective-boosted partitive article to fire at long range (it puts half its attribution beyond sixteen tokens).
